paras: The Crisfield riot was an outbreak of violence in Crisfield, Maryland, on August 19 and 20, 1881, in which white men beat a Black man named Tucker, a white man named George Holland was shot in Goodsell's Alley, and a white crowd the next night took over the alley and fired on its Black residents. An elderly Black man was wounded and no arrests were reported, though a reward of up to $500 was later offered. Accounts in the Snow Hill and Baltimore papers differed over how the shooting began.

According to the Somerset Herald, the trouble began on August 13, when a young man named Coulbourn tried to thrash a Black worker on a scow, and the worker, unable to swim, jumped overboard and was nearly drowned. The Messenger's Crisfield correspondent instead blamed Tucker, "a bright mulatto," for boasting that week of how many white men he could "chew up and spit out," while a Baltimore paper quoted a Captain Wilson blaming drink.

On Friday night, August 19, a crowd of white men including George Holland and his brother John stood outside Blizzard's restaurant when Tucker passed by. Eyewitnesses cited by the Herald said John Holland told Tucker he would "not stay here long" before Tucker was struck on the head. Tucker ran to his house in Goodsell's Alley crying, "Come on boys, they have nearly murdered me," and at least a score of Black residents, the correspondent wrote, "began a reckless, indiscriminate firing down the alley." Holland was hit in the abdomen.

On Saturday, leaders of the whites threatened to "gut the alley" and "burn the negroes out," and Black residents began leaving town. After dark about 50 white men took "absolute control" of the lower end of the alley and fired pistols "whenever and at whatever they pleased"; an old Black man was shot in the back, his truss turning the ball.

Der Deutsche Correspondent of Baltimore described instead a gang of roughs from the surrounding area who held the town from about 4 to 8 p.m. and fired into houses of Black women and children. In that account a husband whose wife was nearly shot fired back with a double gun, wounding a man printed as "Ekuard Dietze." The same paper later reported that whites had prepared to burn the Black block but were talked out of it.

No arrests were reported as of August 25, and some townspeople criticized the authorities for it. Holland's physicians found the bullet near his spine and judged the wound not serious. The Baltimore paper reported an effort to organize a militia company, and by August 31 a reward of up to $500 had been offered for the arrest and conviction of all concerned; no report of a trial appears in the coverage.

The Democratic Messenger of Snow Hill carried the fullest account on August 27 under the headline "Riot at Crisfield" and the deck "Three Men Shot," though the surviving text names only two. Its correspondent wrote in a mock-heroic style, calling the Black residents "sons of Africa" and "darkies," while also recording the white crowd's free firing. On the same page it reprinted the Somerset Herald's account, which put the first blows with the Hollands and called the riot a "greatly to-be-regretted affair."

Baltimore's German-language Der Deutsche Correspondent headed its report "Gefährliche Ruhestörungen in Crisfield" (dangerous disturbances) and called the attackers roughs, while the Smyrna Times in Delaware gave the riot one line, on the reward.

Holland's part is disputed: the Messenger's correspondent placed him at Tucker's corner with a cocked pistol, and the Herald repeated a rumor that he fired several shots down the alley before being hit from an upstairs window. The Baltimore paper first said he was about to fire when an unknown person shot him, then called him merely a spectator.

reader.title: Crisfield riot (1881)
bases: After whites beat Tucker and a white man was shot in an exchange of fire, a white crowd of about 50 took control of the Black-inhabited Goodsell's Alley, fired pistols at will and threatened to 'burn the negroes out' (A3), and a Baltimore paper reports shots into houses of colored women and children and a plan to burn the Black block (A1, A2).

The Crisfield correspondent of the Snow Hill paper (A3), the Somerset Herald (A4) and the Baltimore German paper (A1, A2) give independent accounts with different details that agree on the Friday shooting of Holland and the Saturday attack on the alley.

accounts.label: Crisfield correspondent (Democratic Messenger)
accounts.gist: Whites beat Tucker, at least a score of Black residents then fired down the alley and hit Holland, who was reportedly at Tucker's corner with a cocked pistol; on Saturday about 50 white men took control of the alley after dark and fired at will.

accounts.label: Somerset Herald
accounts.gist: Traces the trouble to a scow fight on August 13; eyewitnesses say John Holland insulted Tucker before he was struck, and rumor says George Holland fired several shots down the alley before someone in an upstairs window shot back.

accounts.label: Der Deutsche Correspondent (Baltimore)
accounts.gist: Holland was shot by an unknown person as he was about to fire; on Saturday a gang of roughs from the surrounding area held the town from about 4 to 8 p.m. and fired into Black homes; later calls Holland a mere spectator and reports a plan to burn the Black block.

framing.detail: The Messenger's 'Riot at Crisfield' ('Pistols and Shotguns Used—Three Men Shot') mocks the Black residents as 'sons of Africa' and 'darkies' but also reports the white crowd firing 'whenever and at whatever they pleased' and criticism of the authorities.
The Somerset Herald piece reprinted by the Messenger puts the first insult and blows with the Hollands and calls the riot a 'greatly to-be-regretted affair'.
Der Deutsche Correspondent heads its report 'Gefährliche Ruhestörungen in Crisfield' and calls the Saturday attackers roughs and vagabonds who seized the town by force.
The Smyrna Times gave the riot one line, on the reward.
